title: Stationary stochastic finite-armed bandits: expected pseudo-regret.
summary: Each arm has a fixed unknown bounded reward distribution and supplies a fresh sample whenever pulled. Performance uses the true means and compares with the best fixed arm. Observation noise is excluded from the comparator definition.

description_paragraphs: Each arm has a fixed unknown bounded reward distribution and supplies a fresh sample whenever pulled. Performance uses the true means and compares with the best fixed arm. Observation noise is excluded from the comparator definition.

model.instance: Each arm has a fixed unknown distribution nu_i supported on [0,1], with mean mu_i. Selecting arm i produces a fresh independent sample. Cumulative pseudo-regret is computed from the means.

assumptions.scope: The objects, time horizon, and variable blocks explicitly declared here; none is inherited from another specification.
assumptions.description: Each arm has an i.i.d. sample stream. This specification takes streams mutually independent; selecting an arm reveals its next fresh sample.

model.parameter_domain_description: K: $K\in\mathbb N,\ K\ge2$ (public); T: $T\in\mathbb N,\ T\ge1$ (public)
interaction_timing: The action $a_t$ is chosen from the history and private randomness.
A fresh sample $Y_t$ from that arm is observed.
Pseudo-regret uses $\mu_\star-\mu_{a_t}$, while feedback remains only $Y_t$.
model.adversary_information: The unknown distribution or parameter is fixed before interaction. Learner randomness and sample randomness are independent. No adversary changes the distribution round by round from the learner's history.
unresolved_applicability: The current comparison is distribution-free minimax pseudo-regret. Fixed-instance KL asymptotic constants are a different objective.
description_paragraphs: Unknown arm distributions $\nu_i$ generate i.i.d. sample streams for each arm, taken mutually independent in this model. The distributions do not change during interaction.
Distribution mean $\mu_i$, which cannot be queried directly
The sampled arm is $a_t$. Repeating an arm still yields a fresh sample.
Assume $K\ge2$ and $T\ge1$. Rewards lie in $[0,1]$ and actions in $[K]$.
This regret model does not require a unique best arm, and gaps are hidden.

operations.query_signature: Inputs: $t,\ a_t\in[K]$. Timing and visible information follow the specified protocol.
operations.order_convention: order is relative to the current member f_t(x), f(x), or sample F(x;ξ_t) of the named indexed function family and only with respect to x; finite feedback interfaces have no derivative order

feedback_quality.description: Select an arm before drawing its fresh reward. The learner does not observe mu_i, other arms' rewards in the same round, or future samples. No extra within-round resampling is allowed; the same arm may be selected again next round at additional cost.

operations.coupling: Select an arm before drawing its fresh reward. The learner does not observe mu_i, other arms' rewards in the same round, or future samples. No extra within-round resampling is allowed; the same arm may be selected again next round at additional cost.
operations.index_control: The learner selects feasible actions and any probes permitted by the specification. The environment determines current losses, outcomes, or fresh samples. The learner cannot select future rounds.
operations.access_schedule: Interaction follows the sequence in registry.protocols. Current loss feedback is available only after the action is submitted. Any pre-action disclosure of context or advice is specified separately.

public_inputs: Rewards are supported on $[0,1]$; their distributions and means are hidden.
auxiliary_interfaces: No additional access to hidden losses, means, or gradients is available. Projection, sampling, and internal optimization over public domains may have separately recorded computation costs; they are not free loss oracles.
description_paragraphs: Fresh reward sample from the selected arm:
Select an arm before drawing its fresh reward sample.
The learner cannot observe means $\mu_i$, other arms' same-round rewards, or future samples.
No extra resampling is available within a round; the same arm may be selected and charged again in a later round.
Public inputs are $K,T$ and reward support $[0,1]$. Distributions and means are hidden.

output.feasibility: Every loss-bearing action must belong to the action domain. The final output retains the complete action trajectory.
output.allowed_postprocessing: Any measurable computation on received feedback is allowed. No native observation may be added after the budget is exhausted or the algorithm stops.
output.certificate_requirement: Only the stated statistical guarantee is required, not a certificate verifiable through the feedback interface.
description_paragraphs: The output is the complete action trajectory satisfying feasibility and timing requirements. Randomized mixtures may be implemented before acting. Retrospective averages or convex combinations cannot replace actions that have already incurred loss. No additional optimal value or certificate is required.

metric.normalization: Use the cumulative quantity over T rounds without dividing by T. Preserve the displayed order of probability or expectation.
metric.finiteness_conditions: The compared mean losses or rewards lie in $[0,1]$, so cumulative pseudo-regret lies in $[0,T]$.
description_paragraphs:
$$
Y_t\sim\nu_{a_t},\quad \mu_i=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_i}Y,\quad R_T=\sum_{t=1}^T(\mu_* -\mu_{a_t}),\quad \mu_* =\max_i\mu_i
$$

components.description: Sequential online rounds; only information permitted by the protocol is visible in each round.
One arm pull and one scalar sample per round, under fixed budget T.

resource.budget_semantics: There are T sequential interaction rounds. Native feedback count is determined by the per-round protocol and is not an independent budget to minimize.
resource.scalarization: Retain the native objective and complete resource vector. At fixed $T$, compare cumulative regret. Best-arm-identification stopping times and error probabilities use their own task-specific criteria.
resource.setup_cost: Only declared public inputs may be read. Hidden losses, means, or samples cannot be accessed in advance or outside the $T$ rounds or $\tau$ samples.
resource.online_cost: Any causal randomized policy is allowed, and MOSS provides a verified upper bound. Maintaining arm averages, counts, and selection indices is charged separately from the T reward observations.
resource.amortization_scope: The algorithm runs on one environment. Charged feedback cannot be reused across independent instances.
resource.precision_model: Observations and internal arithmetic use the exact-real model. No bit-complexity claim follows.
description_paragraphs: One arm pull and one scalar sample per round, under fixed budget T.
Arbitrary causal randomized policies are allowed; MOSS is the admitted upper-bound algorithm.
Maintain arm sample means, counts, and selection indices. These internal operations are charged separately from the T reward samples.

Information calls, arithmetic, communication rounds, and memory are measured separately. Exact real internal computation is excluded from information complexity unless explicitly charged. This does not imply a bit-complexity bound.

algorithms.randomization: Private randomization is allowed. The seed is hidden from the environment and independent of the fixed instance and sample randomness.
algorithms.adaptivity: The action and every probe in a round may depend only on previous-round feedback, public inputs, any context or advice already revealed that round, and private randomness. They may not use unrevealed current losses or samples.
restrictions: All measurable causal policies satisfying the declared information timing and feasible domain are allowed, without extra span, iteration-form, or polynomial-time restrictions.
algorithms.internal_computation: Arbitrary measurable policies and exact internal arithmetic are allowed. Feedback complexity alone does not determine arithmetic or bit complexity. MOSS provides a verified upper bound within the class of causal randomized policies. Maintaining arm averages, counts, and selection indices is charged separately from the T reward observations.
algorithms.parallelism: Interaction proceeds in sequential time rounds. A two-point evaluation is one pair of same-round responses only where explicitly permitted; it is not equivalent to two independent rounds.
description_paragraphs: All measurable causal randomized policies respecting the stated timing are allowed. The private seed is independent of the fixed instance and future samples. Apart from explicit feedback, output, and budget requirements, there are no restrictions on linear spans, iteration form, internal arithmetic, memory, or communication.

bounds.derivation: The source bounds expected realized regret. If $X_{t,i}$ is arm $i$'s reward, then $\mathbb E\max_i\sum_tX_{t,i}\ge\max_i\mathbb E\sum_tX_{t,i}$. Its expected-realized-regret upper bound therefore controls this pseudo-regret. Only this direction of transfer is used.

evidence.supports: The source supports $\mathcal{R}_T^*\ge0.04\sqrt{KT}$ and the stated reductions, subject to each atomic claim's model, feedback, parameter region, and quantifiers.
notes: Use only the K-armed bandit branch with source sampling budget $m_{\mathrm{src}}=T$. In context-block reductions each block uses its own length. Bernoulli hard instances and Yao's principle give the randomized-learner lower bound.

evidence.supports: Source support for the listed results and necessary explicit transfers: $\mathcal{R}_T^*\le25\sqrt{KT}$. Applicability is restricted separately by each atomic bound's model, feedback, regime, and quantifiers.
notes: For fixed arm distributions supported on $[0,1]$, the source gives expected realized regret at most $25\sqrt{KT}$. The inequality between expectation and maximization implies the same upper bound for pseudo-regret.
